newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia opposition faces sedition verdict.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia opposition faces sedition verdict.

text.p: Malaysia's paltry opposition in Parliament could shrink even further next week if one of its leaders is convicted of sedition at a time when Malaysian activist groups are under fire.
A High Court judge in west coast Malacca state is due to deliver a verdict on April 28 in the case against Lim Guan Eng, youth chairman of the minority Democratic Action Party (DAP).

"I'm not very optimistic," said Lim, who could be jailed for up to six years, fined thousands of dollars and disqualified from Parliament if convicted of making false statements against Malacca's chief minister.
His is not the only case to prompt debate over whether there is a larger pattern of intolerance in Malaysia against dissent and official alarm at the growing influence of activist groups.

Irene Fernandez, head of the labour rights group Tenaganita, is also on trial in a Kuala Lumpur courtroom on sedition charges. She is accused of making false statements that illegal immigrants were dying at a detention camp.

Last November, a mob of youths from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) stormed into a Kuala Lumpur hotel, forcibly ending a seminar on Indonesia's occupation of East Timor.
Conference participants were arrested and their foreign guests deported. Several of the UMNO youth were also detained.
The thuggish action was roundly condemned even by government supporters and became an international embarrassment.
NGOS ALLOWED MORE SPACE

"There isn't any systematic attempt to hound the oppositon or stifle dissent," said Chandra Muzzafar, head of the human rights group JUST and a veteran of battles between non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and the government.
"The last six years or so (NGOs) have been allowed more space and scope for their activities," Chandra, a political science professor at Malaya University, said in an interview.
"You find there's more dialogue with NGOs at government ministries then ever before." A decade ago some 100 government critics were detained during racial tension.
But in January officials from the Registry of Companies raided the offices of three activist groups after Mahathir accused NGOs of using companies as fronts to criticise the government.

NGOs by law must register with the government under the Societies Act, but that can take years. The Malaysian chapter of the human rights group Amnesty International has been waiting five years for certification.
Many NGOs register as trading companies instead because the procedures are far simpler.

Mahathir has been particularly angered by a coalition of NGOs that opposes construction of the $5.5 billion Bakun hydro-electric dam as environmentally and economically unsound and calls it a bad risk for investors.
"They should watch their own backs," Mahathir told reporters on Tuesday. "They are being used by foreigners."
The case against Lim Guan Eng, son of veteran opposition leader Lim Kit Siang, has drawn most attention, however.
London-based Amnesty International said in a recent statement the charges were "politically motivated, designed to intimidate dissenting voices and to limit debate on an issue of public concern".
Lim is charged with making false statements in 1995 about Malacca's Chief Minister Rahim Tamby Chik.
"IMPRISONED VICTIM"

A then 15-year-old schoolgirl accused Rahim of having an affair with her. He denied the accusation and was never charged, but the girl was kept in protective custody by police for eight days for questioning.
Lim alleged she was an "imprisoned victim", a statement the prosecution contended was seditious.
"This is a concerted effort not only against the opposition but against the NGOs," Lim said in an interview. "I think the government realises the NGOs do them harm internationally."
The opposition holds 30 seats in the 192-seat parliament. The DAP with nine seats is the largest opposition party.

The charges against Lim "appear to be part of an established government strategy of selectively using repressive laws in prominent cases to engender a wider public reluctance to criticise the authorities," Amnesty said.
In December, a planned forum on police abuse was cancelled after the government threatened the organisers with the Internal Security Act, which allows indefinite detention without charge.

But despite the official pressure, diplomats and analysts say demonstrations have become more frequent, activist groups have grown stronger and dissenting voices more strident in rapidly modernising Malaysia.
Even Marina Mahathir, daughter of the prime minister and president of the Malaysian AIDS Council, defends the NGOs, saying it is their duty to raise unpopular issues.
"We're not trying to be contrary," she said in the Star newspaper recently. "Who else is going to bring it up."
